user.title: What kind of pool is this?
user.description: These answers decide which questions the rest of the setup asks.

data_description.unit_system: Calculations stay metric either way; this only changes how doses and volumes are shown.
data_description.sanitiser: Determines which readings are worth asking for. Showing a bromine field to a chlorine pool is a field you would wonder about, leave blank, and then see reported as missing.
data_description.pool_kind: An uninsulated inflatable loses heat several times faster than a built-in pool. A frame pool like Intex Metal Frame sits in between. Pick the one that matches your pool — it is only a starting point, and the real figure is measured within days.
data_description.has_solar_collector: Tick if you have a solar collector alongside another heater.
data_description.name: How this pool appears in Home Assistant.

pump.title: Circulation pump
pump.description: With a filter in line roughly {derate}% of the rated flow remains. Have you measured the real flow? Tick the box.

data.pump_flow_measured: This is a measured value, not from the datasheet

data_description.pump_flow_m3h: On the pump label or in the manual, often written as 'flow rate' in m³/h or litres per hour. Divide L/h by 1000 for m³/h. Example: a small cartridge pump is around 2-4 m³/h.
data_description.pump_flow_measured: Tick only if you measured it with a flow meter. Otherwise the datasheet figure is reduced by 30% to account for filter resistance.
data_description.pump_power_kw: On the label, in watts. Divide by 1000. Example: 100 W is 0.1 kW.
data_description.filter_media: Only used to estimate real flow when you have not measured it. Filter balls flow more freely than sand when fresh, but they compress over time and a matted bed chokes the flow badly — a sudden drop means it is time to pull them out and wash them.

entities.title: Required entities
entities.description: The two switches and the pool water temperature. Without these nothing can work.

data_description.pump_switch: The switch or smart plug that powers the circulation pump.
data_description.heat_pump_switch: The switch or smart plug that powers the heat pump.
data_description.water_temp_sensor: The sensor measuring the pool water itself. Take care to pick the right one; it can be changed later under Configure.

optional.title: Optional entities
optional.description: Choose which sensors to add. Every field may be left blank.

menu_options.optional_sensors: Core sensors — outdoor temp, flow, weather
menu_options.optional_solar: Solar and price — solar production, cheap price signal

data_description.air_temp_sensor: Outdoor air at the installation. Without it the operating envelope cannot be checked and frost protection falls back on the weather entity.
data_description.hp_inlet_sensor: Water going into the heat pump. If nothing sits between the pump and the heat pump in your plumbing, this is often the same physical point as "Pump outlet temperature" above — point both fields at that one entity in that case rather than leaving this blank.
data_description.hp_outlet_sensor: Water coming out of the heat pump. Together with the inlet this gives delta-T and COP.
data_description.flow_sensor: A flow meter in m³/h. Enables flow protection and makes the filtration blocks correct themselves as the filter fouls.
data_description.pump_power_sensor: Power draw of the pump, if your plug measures it.
data_description.hp_power_sensor: Power draw of the heat pump, if your plug measures it. Needed for cost and measured COP.
data_description.price_sensor: A sensor whose state is the price per kWh. Dynamic tariff integrations provide this.
data_description.irradiance_sensor: Direct sunlight reading in W/m² — a weather station's pyranometer, a KNMI-style solar-radiation entity, or similar. Preferred over the solar power sensor below when both are mapped: it needs no peak figure to scale against, and works whether or not this pool has solar panels of its own. Used to learn heat loss from sunny idle periods instead of discarding them.
data_description.solar_forecast_sensor: A solar forecast, if you have one.
data_description.weather_entity: Used as a fallback when no outdoor sensor is configured.
data_description.cover_entity: A cover sensor, a switch, or an input_boolean you flip yourself. Heat loss is then learned separately for covered and uncovered, because averaging the two produces a figure that is wrong in both states — a cover typically halves the loss or better.
data_description.flow_unit: Only used when the sensor does not state its own unit. Most pool flow meters report litres per minute; 2 m³/h is 33 L/min.
data_description.cheap_price_sensor: An on/off sensor that says whether now is a cheap moment, published by most dynamic tariff integrations. It outranks the fixed price ceiling because it knows where this hour sits within today's prices: a day whose cheapest hour is above your limit would otherwise never heat, and a cheap hour on an expensive day would be missed.
data_description.pump_inlet_sensor: Water on its way out of the pool, before the pump. It measures the same water as the pool probe, so the two should agree — and when they do not, either a probe needs calibrating, the pool is stratified from too little circulation, or a probe is not in the water. This is the only check able to notice a reading that is simply wrong.
data_description.ph_sensor: A sensor or input_number holding your last pH measurement. Used to work out how much to add, using the pool volume you entered.
data_description.chlorine_sensor: A sensor or input_number holding your last free chlorine measurement in mg/L.
data_description.pump_outlet_sensor: Water leaving the circulation pump, on its way to the heat pump. Kept separate from the heat pump inlet below because that assumes only one plumbing layout: if there is a filter, a longer run, or anything else between the pump and the heat pump, these are two real points. If your plumbing runs pool → pump → heat pump → pool with nothing in between, and you only have one probe there, point this field and "Heat pump inlet temperature" at the same entity — the integration recognises they are one measurement and will not compare them against each other as if they were independent.
data_description.total_chlorine_sensor: Total chlorine minus free chlorine gives combined chlorine — the part already used up by contamination. Above 0.5 mg/L, shocking does more than topping up. It is the one figure a strip gives you that answers 'should I shock', and it only exists if two columns are subtracted.
data_description.bromine_sensor: Only if you sanitise with bromine instead of chlorine. The two are alternatives, not additions.
data_description.alkalinity_sensor: The buffer that holds pH steady. Out of range, pH drifts on its own and correcting it is a weekly chore rather than a fix.
data_description.cyanuric_sensor: Stabiliser, which shields chlorine from sunlight. Too little and chlorine burns off in hours; above about 100 ppm it holds chlorine hostage and adding more achieves nothing.
data_description.hardness_sensor: Soft water pulls calcium out of grout and fittings; hard water scales the heat exchanger.
data_description.salt_sensor: Only for a salt chlorinator. The ideal range depends on your cell, so check its manual.
data_description.collector_sensor: A probe at the collector outlet. Without it there is nothing to compare against the pool.

optional_sensors.title: Core sensors
optional_sensors.description: Outdoor temperature, flow, pump data, and the weather and cover entities. Most pools have these sensors.

data_description.air_temp_sensor: Outdoor air at the installation. Frost protection falls back on the weather entity without it.
data_description.pump_inlet_sensor: Water leaving the pool, before the pump. Should match the pool probe.
data_description.pump_outlet_sensor: Water leaving the pump. Difference with inlet = temperature rise.
data_description.flow_sensor: For flow protection and automatic correction as the filter fouls.
data_description.flow_unit: Only needed if the sensor does not state its own unit.
data_description.pump_power_sensor: Power draw of the pump (if your plug measures it).
data_description.price_sensor: Sensor with the price per kWh. Needed for price optimisation.
data_description.weather_entity: Fallback when no outdoor sensor is configured.
data_description.cover_entity: Cover, switch or input_boolean. Heat loss is learned separately covered/uncovered.
data_description.hp_inlet_sensor: Water going into the heat pump.
data_description.hp_outlet_sensor: Water coming out of the heat pump. Together with inlet = COP.
data_description.hp_power_sensor: Power draw of the heat pump. Needed for cost and COP.

optional_chemistry.title: Water chemistry
optional_chemistry.description: pH, chlorine, bromine, alkalinity, cyanuric acid, hardness, and salt. These can be sensors or input_number helpers you update after a test.

data_description.ph_sensor: A sensor or input_number with your last pH reading.
data_description.chlorine_sensor: A sensor or input_number with your last free chlorine reading.
data_description.total_chlorine_sensor: Total minus free chlorine = combined chlorine. Above 0.5 mg/L, shocking helps more.
data_description.bromine_sensor: Only if you sanitise with bromine instead of chlorine.
data_description.cyanuric_sensor: Stabiliser that shields chlorine from sunlight.
data_description.hardness_sensor: Too soft pulls calcium from grout; too hard scales the heat exchanger.

optional_solar.title: Solar and price
optional_solar.description: Solar production, solar forecast, collector temperature, and a cheap-price signal. Only relevant with solar panels or a dynamic tariff.

data_description.irradiance_sensor: A sensor already reading in W/m², such as a weather station's pyranometer or a KNMI-style solar-radiation entity. Preferred over the production sensor below when both are set: no peak figure needed, and it works even without solar panels of your own.
data_description.solar_forecast_sensor: Expected solar energy for the coming hours/days.
data_description.collector_sensor: Temperature at the solar collector outlet.
data_description.cheap_price_sensor: Signal indicating whether now is a cheap moment (from a dynamic tariff integration).

optional_finish.title: Done
optional_finish.description: Everything is set up. Choose 'Continue' to review your configuration and save. You can always change settings later via Configure.

summary.title: Review your setup
summary.description: Check your selections below. Click 'Save' to activate PoolSmart. You can always change settings later via Configure.

adopt.title: Learned history found
adopt.description: {count} earlier installation(s) left learned history behind. Adopting it saves rebuilding weeks of measurements.

heating.title: Heating appliance
heating.description: Questions for your heating source. Got a heat pump with its own thermostat? Set it to {recommended_setpoint} °C.

data.hp_cop_low: COP at a second, lower air temperature
data.hp_flow_min_blocking: Pause heating below the minimum flow
data.hp_flow_min_site_verified: Minimum flow verified for this installation

data_description.hp_input_kw: The electricity it draws, on the type plate as 'input power' or 'rated input'. Example: 0.58 kW. Do not confuse this with heat output.
data_description.hp_thermal_kw: The heat it delivers, usually the headline figure such as '3 kW'. Normally 4 to 5 times the input power.
data_description.hp_cop_ref_temp: The air temperature the heat output was measured at. Datasheets usually say 26 °C or 24 °C. If unsure, leave at 26.
data_description.hp_cop_low: Optional. The COP at a colder air temperature, if the datasheet lists a second figure. Leave blank for a flat curve.
data_description.hp_cop_low_temp: The air temperature belonging to that second COP, usually 15 °C.
data_description.hp_air_temp_min: Below this the unit refuses to start. Most pool heat pumps stop somewhere between 10 and 15 °C. If unsure, 11 is a safe guess.
data_description.hp_air_temp_max: Rarely relevant in this climate. 43 °C is a typical limit.
data_description.hp_flow_min_m3h: The datasheet figure, in m³/h. 2 m³/h is 33 L/min. Many installations run below the quoted minimum without trouble, so this only warns unless you switch on the option below. Set it to what your system actually achieves to stop the warnings.
data_description.hp_flow_min_blocking: Off by default. Datasheet minima are conservative and the heat pump has its own flow switch as a hardware backstop, so falling below the figure is reported as a warning rather than stopping the session. Turn this on if you would rather it stopped.
data_description.hp_flow_min_site_verified: Tick if you confirmed your system runs fine below the minimum flow — a normal temperature rise across the heat pump is the evidence.
data_description.collector_margin: Below this difference, water sent through the collector gains too little to be worth circulating — and below zero it actively loses heat.

pool.title: Pool size
pool.description: The volume matters most — every dose and every heating estimate is worked out from it. Depth and surface are used for heat loss and can be left to be derived.

data_description.name: How this pool appears in Home Assistant. Useful if you have more than one.
data_description.volume_l: Printed on the box, or length × width × average depth in metres, × 1000. Getting this right matters more than any other number here: doses and heating times are both calculated from it.
data_description.depth_m: Average, not maximum. For a pool with a sloping floor, halfway between the shallow and deep ends.
data_description.surface_m2: Leave empty and it is worked out from volume and depth. It sets how fast the pool loses heat to the air, and how much sun it takes in.
data_description.target_temp: What the water should be when you swim. Every degree costs roughly an hour and a half of heating on a small pool.
data_description.max_temp: A ceiling the automation will not go past, whatever else it is told. Set it a couple of degrees above the target.

swimming.title: Swimming times
swimming.description: One window per weekday covers nearly every household. The second is there for exceptions and may be left blank.

data_description.swim_time: The planner works backwards from this to decide when heating must start. Leave blank if you have no fixed time; heating then simply keeps the pool at target.
data_description.swim_time_2: A second time on the same days, for the exceptions. Most people leave this empty.
data_description.swim_days: Which weekdays the times above apply to.

notifications.title: Notifications
notifications.description: Choose who receives each kind of message. Select one or more targets per event; the message goes to all of them. Leave blank to use the default target.

data_description.default: Where anything without its own destination goes.
data_description.heating_started: Sent when a heating session begins.
data_description.target_reached: Sent when the pool reaches its target temperature.
data_description.flow_fault: Flow problems. Worth routing to whoever fixes things.
data_description.sensor_fault: A sensor stopped reporting or reported something implausible.
data_description.high_energy_cost: Notable price events, including electricity going below zero.
data_description.heating_postponed: Heating is waiting for a cheaper moment.
data_description.ai_recommendation: The weekly review summary, when you run one.
data_description.filter_service: Flow has dropped enough that the filter probably needs cleaning.

data.turnover_factor: Turnover factor (times the pool volume per day)
data.negative_price_basis: Which price counts as below zero
data.stale_warning_seconds: Warn when a reading is older than (seconds)
data.stale_blocking_seconds: Treat a sensor as dead after (seconds)
data.min_daily_hours: Minimum filtration per day at swimming temperature (hours)

data_description.turnover_factor: How many times the whole pool should pass the filter per day. Filtered water mixes back in, so one pass cleans about 63% of the pool, two 86%, three 95%. Three is where the gains flatten off.
data_description.min_daily_hours: A time-based floor, used when it is larger than the turnover figure. Skimming, sanitiser contact and avoiding stagnation all depend on hours running, not on how fast the pump is. This value applies around 25 °C and scales from half of it in cold water to one and a half times above 30 °C.
data_description.min_block_minutes: Runs shorter than this are not worth starting; the water barely reaches the filter.
data_description.night_start: Quiet hours begin. Only safety, the filtration deadline, a negative price or a manual boost run after this.
data_description.min_on_minutes: Once something switches on it stays on at least this long. This is what stops the pump chattering.
data_description.min_off_minutes: Once something switches off it stays off at least this long.
data_description.pump_rundown_minutes: The pump keeps circulating this long after the heat pump stops, to carry the residual heat away from it.
data_description.temp_hysteresis: How far below target the water must fall before heating restarts. Stopping happens exactly at target.
data_description.min_water_temp: Below this the pool is protected regardless of mode. If the air is too cold for the heat pump, protection circulates instead of heating.
data_description.frost_air_temp: Below this outdoor temperature the pump circulates. Moving water does not freeze.
data_description.max_price: Heating waits for a cheaper moment above this price. Boost ignores it. Leave it high to effectively switch price optimisation off.
data_description.negative_price_basis: Which price has to drop below zero before heating runs regardless of everything else.
data_description.solar_threshold_w: Above this, heating is treated as free and the price limit is ignored. Leave empty and it is calculated from what the heat pump and pump draw together, plus the margin below. A figure lower than the equipment draw means exporting less than you use; much higher means missing sunny afternoons.
data_description.solar_hysteresis_w: Extra margin required in ECO mode, so passing clouds do not start and stop a session.
data_description.eco_price_factor: ECO multiplies the price limit by this, making it stricter. 0.7 means ECO only heats below 70% of your normal limit.
data_description.chemistry_cycle_minutes: How long the pump runs when you press the chemistry button.
data_description.stale_warning_seconds: Some sensors only report when their value changes, so a steady temperature can look old. This is when to start mentioning it.
data_description.stale_blocking_seconds: When to treat the sensor as dead and pause heating. Circulation and filtration continue.
data_description.learning_enabled: Whether finished sessions update the heating rate, heat loss and COP figures.
data_description.pump_startup_grace_seconds: Flow is not judged for this long after the pump starts. The pump has to prime and push the air out of the lines, and reporting that as a fault turns a normal start into an alarm.
data_description.solar_margin_w: Added to the equipment draw when the threshold is calculated. A margin stops a passing cloud from starting and stopping a session.
data_description.compressor_min_off_minutes: How long the heat pump must stay off before restarting, so refrigerant pressures can equalise. Short cycling wears a compressor out early. This cannot be overridden by any other rule.
data_description.compressor_min_on_minutes: Minimum run once started. Reaching the target temperature still stops it immediately.
data_description.calibration_tolerance: How far the pool probe and the pump inlet may differ before it is mentioned. DS18B20s are accurate to roughly ±0.5 °C, so anything under that is the sensors rather than the pool.
data_description.tablet_grams: The size your chlorine tablets actually come in — commonly 20 g, 200 g or 500 g. Tablets are counted rather than weighed out, so this is what turns a required weight into a number of tablets.

data_description.target_temp: 28 °C is comfortable for most people. 26 is brisk, 30 is bath-like and noticeably more expensive.

weather_price.title: Weather and price
weather_price.description: Everything read from outside the pool: the weather, the electricity price, and the sun. Clearing an optional field switches that feature off again.

data_description.weather_entity: A weather entity with a forecast. Used to scale the learned heat loss to the temperature ahead, so a cold front starts the heating plan earlier and a warm spell is not over-heated for.
data_description.air_temp_sensor: Outdoor air at the installation. Without it the operating envelope cannot be checked and frost protection falls back on the weather entity.
data_description.price_sensor: A sensor whose state is the price per kWh. Dynamic tariff integrations provide this.

data_description.irradiance_sensor: Direct sunlight reading in W/m² — a weather station's pyranometer, a KNMI-style solar-radiation entity, or similar. Preferred over the solar power sensor above when both are mapped: it needs no peak figure to scale against, and works whether or not this pool has solar panels of its own. Used to learn heat loss from sunny idle periods instead of discarding them.
data_description.grid_power_sensor: A smart-meter or energy-dashboard sensor reading total household power in watts, independent of the pool's own equipment. Paired with the house power limit under When to heat to pause heating above a cap — useful for peak tariffs or a grid/contract limit. Leave blank and the limiter is simply absent.

data.hp_cop_low: COP at a second, lower air temperature
data.hp_flow_min_blocking: Pause heating below the minimum flow
data.hp_flow_min_site_verified: Minimum flow verified for this installation

data_description.pool_kind: Sets a realistic starting figure for heat loss — an uninsulated inflatable loses several times faster than a built-in pool. It is only a starting point; the real figure is measured within days.
data_description.heating_source: Changes which questions follow. A solar collector is usually on a manual three-way valve, so the integration advises when to open it rather than switching anything.
data_description.has_solar_collector: Tick if you have a collector alongside another heater. Free heat is always preferred over paid heat.
data_description.collector_sensor: A probe at the collector outlet. Without it there is nothing to compare against the pool.
data_description.collector_margin: Below this difference, water sent through the collector gains too little to be worth circulating — and below zero it actively loses heat.
data_description.hp_air_temp_max: Rarely relevant in this climate. 43 °C is a typical limit.
data_description.hp_air_temp_min: Below this the unit refuses to start. Most pool heat pumps stop somewhere between 10 and 15 °C. If unsure, 11 is a safe guess.
data_description.hp_cop_low: Optional. The COP at a colder air temperature, if the datasheet lists a second figure. Leave blank for a flat curve.
data_description.hp_cop_low_temp: The air temperature belonging to that second COP, usually 15 °C.
data_description.hp_cop_ref_temp: The air temperature the heat output was measured at. Datasheets usually say 26 °C or 24 °C. If unsure, leave at 26.
data_description.hp_flow_min_blocking: Off by default. Datasheet minima are conservative and the heat pump has its own flow switch as a hardware backstop, so falling below the figure is reported as a warning rather than stopping the session. Turn this on if you would rather it stopped.
data_description.hp_flow_min_m3h: The datasheet figure, in m³/h. 2 m³/h is 33 L/min. Many installations run below the quoted minimum without trouble, so this only warns unless you switch on the option below. Set it to what your system actually achieves to stop the warnings.
data_description.hp_flow_min_site_verified: Tick if you confirmed your system runs fine below the minimum flow — a normal temperature rise across the heat pump is the evidence.
data_description.hp_input_kw: The electricity it draws, on the type plate as 'input power' or 'rated input'. Example: 0.58 kW. Do not confuse this with heat output.
data_description.hp_thermal_kw: The heat it delivers, usually the headline figure such as '3 kW'. Normally 4 to 5 times the input power.
data_description.hp_cop_ref: How many kilowatts of heat you get per kilowatt of electricity, at the outdoor temperature below. From the datasheet — but the integration measures your own within a few sessions and prefers that, because a figure measured on your installation beats one measured on a test bench.

when_to_heat.title: When to heat
when_to_heat.description: Target temperatures, swimming time, and what makes heating worth doing — price and sun.

data.cheap_price_ceiling: Cheap-period signal's own ceiling (per kWh, optional)
data.negative_price_basis: Which price counts as below zero

data_description.eco_price_factor: ECO multiplies the price limit by this, making it stricter. 0.7 means ECO only heats below 70% of your normal limit.
data_description.frost_air_temp: Below this outdoor temperature the pump circulates. Moving water does not freeze.
data_description.max_price: Heating waits for a cheaper moment above this price. Boost ignores it. Leave it high to effectively switch price optimisation off.
data_description.cheap_price_mode: Only relevant with a cheap-period signal mapped under Weather and price. 'Always wins' lets the signal heat above the maximum price, because it knows the shape of today's prices and a fixed ceiling does not. 'Hard ceiling' makes the maximum price a promise nothing crosses, so a 'cheap' hour that is still above it is treated like any other expensive hour. 'Own ceiling' keeps the signal authoritative but adds a separate, usually higher, price below it that even the signal may not cross.
data_description.cheap_price_ceiling: Only used when the option above is set to 'own ceiling'. The cheap-period signal is trusted below this price; above it, heating is judged the normal way. Leave blank to make that option behave like 'always wins'.
data_description.max_temp: The highest you would ever set. Used to suggest a safe setting for the heat pump's own thermostat.
data_description.min_water_temp: Below this the pool is protected regardless of mode. If the air is too cold for the heat pump, protection circulates instead of heating.
data_description.negative_price_basis: Which price has to drop below zero before heating runs regardless of everything else.
data_description.solar_hysteresis_w: Extra margin required in ECO mode, so passing clouds do not start and stop a session.
data_description.solar_margin_w: Added to the equipment draw when the threshold is calculated. A margin stops a passing cloud from starting and stopping a session.
data_description.solar_peak_w: The panel array's rated peak output. Used to scale the solar production sensor into an estimated W/m² irradiance when no direct irradiance sensor is mapped under Entities. Leave blank if you have no solar panels, or if the irradiance sensor already covers it.
data_description.solar_threshold_w: Above this, heating is treated as free and the price limit is ignored. Leave empty and it is calculated from what the heat pump and pump draw together, plus the margin below. A figure lower than the equipment draw means exporting less than you use; much higher means missing sunny afternoons.
data_description.power_limit_w: Heating pauses whenever the house's total draw (plus the pool's own equipment, if not already running) would exceed this. Requires a house power sensor under Weather and price. Even Boost respects it, since it exists to protect a hard electrical or contract limit. Leave blank and there is no cap.
data_description.swim_time: The planner works backwards from this to decide when heating must start. Leave blank if you have no fixed time; heating then simply keeps the pool at target.
data_description.swim_time_2: A second time on the same days, for the exceptions. Most people leave this empty.
data_description.swim_days: Which weekdays the times above apply to.
data_description.swim_time_entity: An input_datetime helper you put on your dashboard, so anyone in the house can set today's time without opening this screen. Checked before the fixed time above, and ignored when left blank.
data_description.swim_skip_entity: An input_boolean helper for "not swimming today" — flip it on the dashboard to skip today without changing the schedule.
data_description.target_temp: 28 °C is comfortable for most people. 26 is brisk, 30 is bath-like and noticeably more expensive.

filtration.title: Filtration
filtration.description: How much circulation the pool needs each day, and when it may happen.

data.min_daily_hours: Minimum filtration per day at swimming temperature (hours)
data.turnover_factor: Turnover factor (times the pool volume per day)

data_description.min_block_minutes: Runs shorter than this are not worth starting; the water barely reaches the filter.
data_description.min_daily_hours: A time-based floor, used when it is larger than the turnover figure. Skimming, sanitiser contact and avoiding stagnation all depend on hours running, not on how fast the pump is. This value applies around 25 °C and scales from half of it in cold water to one and a half times above 30 °C.
data_description.night_start: Quiet hours begin. Only safety, the filtration deadline, a negative price or a manual boost run after this.
data_description.pump_rundown_minutes: The pump keeps circulating this long after the heat pump stops, to carry the residual heat away from it.
data_description.turnover_factor: How many times the whole pool should pass the filter per day. Filtered water mixes back in, so one pass cleans about 63% of the pool, two 86%, three 95%. Three is where the gains flatten off.

water.title: Water treatment
water.description: Which products you use, so a reading becomes an amount you can measure out.

data_description.chemistry_cycle_minutes: How long the pump runs when you press the chemistry button.
data_description.filter_media: Only used to estimate real flow when you have not measured it. Filter balls flow more freely than sand when fresh, but they compress over time and a matted bed chokes the flow badly — a sudden drop means it is time to pull them out and wash them.
data_description.sanitiser: Determines which readings are worth asking for. Showing a bromine field to a chlorine pool is a field you would wonder about, leave blank, and then see reported as missing.
data_description.tablet_grams: The size your chlorine tablets actually come in — commonly 20 g, 200 g or 500 g. Tablets are counted rather than weighed out, so this is what turns a required weight into a number of tablets.
data_description.ph_sensor: A sensor or input_number holding your last pH measurement. Used to work out how much to add, using the pool volume you entered.
data_description.chlorine_sensor: A sensor or input_number holding your last free chlorine measurement in mg/L.
data_description.total_chlorine_sensor: Total chlorine minus free chlorine gives combined chlorine — the part already used up by contamination. Above 0.5 mg/L, shocking does more than topping up. It is the one figure a strip gives you that answers 'should I shock', and it only exists if two columns are subtracted.
data_description.bromine_sensor: Only if you sanitise with bromine instead of chlorine. The two are alternatives, not additions.
data_description.alkalinity_sensor: The buffer that holds pH steady. Out of range, pH drifts on its own and correcting it is a weekly chore rather than a fix.
data_description.cyanuric_sensor: Stabiliser, which shields chlorine from sunlight. Too little and chlorine burns off in hours; above about 100 ppm it holds chlorine hostage and adding more achieves nothing.
data_description.hardness_sensor: Soft water pulls calcium out of grout and fittings; hard water scales the heat exchanger.
data_description.salt_sensor: Only for a salt chlorinator. The ideal range depends on your cell, so check its manual.

advanced.title: Advanced
advanced.description: Things you only change when a measurement misbehaves. Sensible defaults are already in place.

data.stale_blocking_seconds: Treat a sensor as dead after (seconds)
data.stale_warning_seconds: Warn when a reading is older than (seconds)

data_description.calibration_tolerance: How far the pool probe and the pump inlet may differ before it is mentioned. DS18B20s are accurate to roughly ±0.5 °C, so anything under that is the sensors rather than the pool.
data_description.compressor_min_off_minutes: How long the heat pump must stay off before restarting, so refrigerant pressures can equalise. Short cycling wears a compressor out early. This cannot be overridden by any other rule.
data_description.compressor_min_on_minutes: Minimum run once started. Reaching the target temperature still stops it immediately.
data_description.learning_enabled: Whether finished sessions update the heating rate, heat loss and COP figures.
data_description.min_off_minutes: Once something switches off it stays off at least this long.
data_description.min_on_minutes: Once something switches on it stays on at least this long. This is what stops the pump chattering.
data_description.pump_startup_grace_seconds: Flow is not judged for this long after the pump starts. The pump has to prime and push the air out of the lines, and reporting that as a fault turns a normal start into an alarm.
data_description.stale_blocking_seconds: When to treat the sensor as dead and pause heating. Circulation and filtration continue.
data_description.stale_warning_seconds: Some sensors only report when their value changes, so a steady temperature can look old. This is when to start mentioning it.
data_description.temp_hysteresis: How far below target the water must fall before heating restarts. Stopping happens exactly at target.
data_description.max_step_ratio: How far a learned value may move in one go, as a fraction. At 0.15 a single odd session shifts things by at most fifteen percent, so one bad measurement cannot undo weeks of good ones. Lower is steadier and slower to adapt.
data_description.hp_cop_clamp_min: A session whose measured COP falls below this is treated as a bad reading and left out of the automatic verdict, whatever review state it carries. Raise this only if your heat pump's genuine efficiency runs lower than the default 3.0 allows for.
data_description.hp_cop_clamp_max: The same ceiling on the high side. A measured COP above this is treated as a bad reading rather than an unusually efficient session. Also caps the planning curve, so this affects predictions as well as which sessions teach the model.

options.total: All-in price below zero (rare, but you genuinely earn money)
options.market: Spot price below zero (more often, but you still pay taxes)

options.max_price_hard: Maximum price is a hard ceiling
options.cheap_wins_capped: Cheap-period signal wins, up to its own ceiling

options.none: No heating — filtration and water only

options.inflatable: Inflatable — inflated ring holding the walls up
options.frame: Frame pool — steel frame with liner, like Intex Metal Frame
options.above_ground: Above ground — solid steel or timber walls, stays up all year
options.in_ground: In ground — built into the ground
